title: GOMER IS MORE THAN A SERMON ILLUSTRATION ABOUT AN “UNFAITHFUL WOMAN”
paragraphs:
GOMER IS MORE THAN A SERMON ILLUSTRATION ABOUT AN “UNFAITHFUL WOMAN”
We Have Spent Centuries Looking at Her Shame. Hosea Was Written to Make Us Recognize Ours.
There is something dangerously comfortable about preaching Gomer as though she were somebody else.
The immoral woman.
The adulteress.
The scandal.
The woman who wandered while a faithful man kept loving her.
We hear her name and instinctively stand beside Hosea.
We imagine ourselves among the faithful.
We look across the sanctuary at Gomer.
And perhaps that is exactly where the book of Hosea begins dismantling us.
Because Gomer was never placed in Scripture merely so respectable people could shake their heads at an unfaithful woman.
She became part of a prophetic sign aimed directly at the covenant people of God.
At worshipers.
At people who knew God's name.
At people who could still participate in religion while their hearts belonged somewhere else.
And if you read Hosea long enough, an uncomfortable realization begins crawling beneath your skin:
You were never supposed to watch Gomer from a safe distance.
You were supposed to recognize yourself.
The opening command is shocking even in Hebrew.
God tells Hosea:
“לֵךְ קַח־לְךָ אֵשֶׁת זְנוּנִים”
Lekh, qach-lekha eshet zenunim.
“Go, take for yourself a wife of whoredom.”

The expression eshet zenunim is severe. The noun zenunim belongs to the Hebrew vocabulary of sexual unfaithfulness or prostitution. But the verse immediately tells us why this marriage is being used prophetically:
“כִּי־זָנֹה תִזְנֶה הָאָרֶץ מֵאַחֲרֵי יְהוָה”
“For the land commits great whoredom by forsaking the LORD.”
—Hosea 1:2
That final clause changes how we must read everything.
The deepest scandal in the opening chapter is not merely the sexual history of a woman.
It is the spiritual adultery of a people.
Israel belonged to Yahweh and pursued other gods.
The nation received His provision and attributed His gifts elsewhere. Later God says of Israel, “She did not know that it was I who gave her the grain, the wine, and the oil” (Hosea 2:8).
Read that slowly.
God gave.
Someone else received the credit.
And suddenly Hosea stops feeling ancient.
Because idolatry does not always look like bowing before a carved statue.
Sometimes it looks like needing human approval more than God's approval.
Sometimes it is the relationship you know is dragging you from Christ but refuse to surrender.
Sometimes it is money.
Sometimes pornography.
Sometimes status.
Sometimes resentment.
Sometimes ministry itself.
Sometimes we want God's gifts while quietly resenting God's authority.
We pray when frightened, praise when blessed, disappear when comfortable, return when shattered—and somehow still imagine Gomer is the shocking character in this story.
But Hosea will not let us remain spectators.
Gomer is named in Hosea 1:3:
“וַיֵּלֶךְ וַיִּקַּח אֶת־גֹּמֶר בַּת־דִּבְלָיִם”
“So he went and took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim.”
She becomes Hosea's wife.
Children are born.
And their names become sermons walking through Israel.
Jezreel.
Lo-Ruhamah.
Lo-Ammi.
The final two are particularly devastating.
Lo-Ruhamah carries the sense of “No Mercy” or “Not Pitied.”
Lo-Ammi means “Not My People.”
Imagine hearing a mother calling those names home at sunset.
Imagine children carrying the judgment of a nation in their introductions.
“What is your name?”
“Not My People.”
Yet this is where Hosea becomes astonishing.
Judgment does not get the last word.
Almost immediately after “Not My People,” God announces a future reversal:
“In the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ it shall be said to them, ‘Children of the living God.’”
—Hosea 1:10
That is the heartbeat beneath the wreckage.
God exposes sin because sin destroys what He loves.
Biblical grace does not pretend betrayal never happened.
Grace tells the truth about the wound...
and then does something human beings rarely expect.
God begins speaking restoration over the guilty.
Hosea 2 moves through accusation, judgment, discipline and then into one of Scripture's most breathtaking turns.
God says:
“לָכֵן הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי מְפַתֶּיהָ”
“Therefore, behold, I will allure her...”
And He says He will bring her into the wilderness and speak tenderly to her.
—Hosea 2:14
Did you notice the word?
Therefore.
We expect:
Therefore, I will destroy her.
Therefore, I will humiliate her.
Therefore, I will never speak her name again.
Instead...
God pursues.
Not because sin does not matter.
Precisely because covenant love does.
Then comes language so beautiful that it almost sounds impossible after everything preceding it:
“וְאֵרַשְׂתִּיךְ לִי לְעוֹלָם”
Ve'erastikh li le'olam.
“I will betroth you to Me forever.”
And again:
“וְאֵרַשְׂתִּיךְ לִי בֶּאֱמוּנָה”
“I will betroth you to Me in faithfulness.”
Not merely tolerate you.
Not merely keep you around as permanent evidence of your worst season.
Betroth you.
The language moves toward renewed covenant relationship.
Righteousness.
Justice.
Steadfast love.
Mercy.
Faithfulness.
This does not make sin small.
It makes grace enormous.
And then Hosea 3 opens with another disturbing command.
“Go again, love a woman who is loved by another man and is an adulteress...”
—Hosea 3:1
Here we need to be careful with Scripture.

Hosea 3 does not explicitly call this woman Gomer by name. She has traditionally been understood by many interpreters to be Gomer, and that reading naturally connects chapters 1 and 3, but we should not present an inference as though the verse itself names her.
What the text makes unmistakable is the meaning of Hosea's commanded love.
The verse continues by comparing it with the LORD's love for Israel even while Israel turns toward other gods.
Then Hosea says:
“וָאֶכְּרֶהָ לִּי בַּחֲמִשָּׁה עָשָׂר כָּסֶף”
“So I bought her for fifteen shekels of silver...”
—Hosea 3:2
The exact circumstances behind that transaction are not explained.
Scripture does not tell us enough to reconstruct every detail of what happened to the woman.
Was this payment connected with slavery, debt, marital arrangements, or another ancient economic circumstance?
The text does not fully tell us.
And we should resist the temptation to manufacture cinematic details Scripture never gives.
The Bible's actual words are powerful enough.
Hosea pays a price.
He brings the woman into a renewed relationship.
And the prophetic meaning points beyond their household toward God and His covenant people.
But for Christians reading Hosea within the whole canon of Scripture, something even greater comes into view.
Because centuries later, another Bridegroom would come for an unfaithful people.
Jesus Christ.
And unlike Hosea, Christ would not purchase His people with silver.
The apostle Peter writes:
Now the story becomes painfully personal.
Because Christianity does not say Jesus died for impressive people who occasionally needed spiritual improvement.
“While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8
Before grace rescued us, sin was not merely around us.
It was in us.
We were not standing safely beside the Redeemer analyzing everybody else's scandal.
We needed redemption.
Every one of us.
That changes how we read Gomer.
It should destroy spiritual superiority.
The church should be the last place on earth where redeemed sinners compete over whose past is least embarrassing.
The Cross has already exposed the truth about us.
Our sin was serious enough that Christ had to die.
And God's mercy is magnificent enough that Christ willingly did.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus does not redeem us so we can return comfortably to the idols that enslaved us.
Grace is not permission to keep running.
Grace calls us home.
Jesus began His public proclamation with a command that modern Christianity sometimes whispers when Scripture says it plainly:
“Repent and believe in the gospel.”
—Mark 1:15
Repentance is not paying God back.
It is turning.
Coming into the light.
Dropping the disguise.
Leaving the idol.
Confessing the sin.
Trusting the Savior.
You may have learned how to look Christian while your heart has been wandering for years.
You can raise your hands and still hide something.
You can quote Scripture and still nurture bitterness.
You can serve in ministry while secretly starving for applause.
You can be married and emotionally belong to someone else.
You can tell everybody God is enough while spending every night desperately trying to make something else fill the emptiness.
You can know worship songs without truly worshiping.
And perhaps the most terrifying form of wandering is the kind nobody notices.
Except God.
But listen carefully:
The God who sees what is hidden is also the God who calls sinners home.
Not through denial.
Not through cheap grace.
Through repentance and redemption.
The Cross proves both realities simultaneously.
Your sin is worse than your excuses say.
God's grace in Christ is greater than your shame says.
Maybe that is why this story hurts.
Some people reading this have spent years believing their worst chapter became their permanent name.
Divorced.
Addicted.
Unfaithful.
Abandoned.
Abuser.
Used.
Lukewarm.
Hypocrite.
Failure.
Too dirty.
Too late.
But Scripture contains a startling pattern of renamed futures.
“Not My People” does not remain the final declaration.
Hosea announces restoration.
And the New Testament later reaches back into Hosea's language when describing God's astonishing mercy and the calling of His people (Romans 9:25–26; 1 Peter 2:10).
That does not mean everybody is automatically reconciled to God regardless of Christ.
The New Testament is relentlessly Christ-centered.
Forgiveness is found in Him.
Reconciliation is through Him.
New life is in Him.
The Gospel does not tell you to rename yourself.
It tells you to come to Jesus.
There is a difference.
Self-reinvention says, “I can become somebody better.”
The Gospel says, “I need a Savior.”
And maybe somebody reading this has reached the end of pretending.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your browser history knows.
Maybe your deleted messages know.
Maybe your spouse suspects.
Maybe your pillow has absorbed prayers you were too ashamed to speak aloud.
Maybe church people know the polished version of you while Jesus knows the exhausted one.
Then stop running.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Come to Christ.
Confess what needs confessing.
Turn from what needs abandoning.
Seek forgiveness where forgiveness needs to be sought.
Bring hidden sin into appropriate, trustworthy Christian accountability.
And believe what the Gospel announces about the crucified and risen Jesus:
There is mercy for repentant sinners.
There is cleansing.
There is reconciliation with God.
There is a new life that cannot be manufactured by pretending harder.
You do not have to make your scandal disappear before approaching Jesus.
You approach Jesus because only He can deal truthfully and finally with your sin.
And perhaps that is the detail we have missed while turning Gomer into a sermon illustration.
The book was never asking us merely:
“How could she do that?”
It was forcing God's people to confront another question:
“How have we?”
Where have I taken God's gifts and forgotten the Giver?
Where have I called Jesus Lord while negotiating privately with an idol?
Where have I demanded grace without repentance?
Where have I judged someone else's visible wreckage while protecting my invisible rebellion?
Where have I mistaken religious activity for covenant faithfulness?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Pray.
Repent.
Talk to Jesus.
And if you need brothers and sisters in Christ to stand with you, comment, “pray for me.”
You do not need to publish the details of your private struggle.
God knows them.
But sometimes three honest words are the first crack in a wall we have spent years constructing.
“Pray for me.”
And if Christ is restoring something you thought was beyond redemption, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Someone reading beneath you may desperately need to discover that Christians are not people who never needed rescuing.
We are people whose hope is Jesus Christ.
Not because forwarding an article earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Jesus cannot be bought, and salvation is God's gift of grace received through faith, not a reward for financial support.
Send it privately to the believer who is tired of pretending.
Send it to the person everybody else has already written off.
Send it even to the skeptic who believes Christianity is only a gathering of respectable people condemning broken ones.
Let them see the Cross.

Saving this article may also matter more than you think. There may come a night when shame begins preaching again, when an old temptation calls your name, or when someone you love confesses something that leaves you unsure how grace and truth can possibly coexist.
Come back to Hosea.
Then go from Hosea to Jesus.
Not as a transaction with God.
Not as proof that you love Jesus.
But as a voluntary way of helping this ministry continue producing and sharing Christ-centered biblical content with people who desperately need it.
If these resources strengthen your walk, consider helping us keep putting biblical truth in front of people who might otherwise never stop long enough to hear it.
Do not merely admire the Gospel.
Respond to Christ.

Because the greatest tragedy would be reading all the way through Gomer's story, feeling emotional about relentless love, sharing the article, commenting on it, saving it, even supporting the ministry...
and still refusing the Savior to whom the story ultimately points.
Jesus is not asking you to become impressive enough to deserve redemption.
He calls sinners to repent and believe.
The Cross is where our excuses die.
The empty tomb is where hopelessness loses its authority.
And grace is not God pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace is God doing what sinners could never accomplish for themselves through Jesus Christ.
So the next time someone says “Gomer,” do not immediately picture somebody else's worst mistake.
Remember Israel.
Remember yourself.
Remember the holiness of God that refuses to call evil good.
Remember the mercy of God that pursues the undeserving.
Remember the blood of Christ.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that the Gospel is not the announcement that your past was harmless.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ is mighty enough to redeem sinners from it.
And comment one sentence if it is genuinely your prayer:
“Jesus, bring my wandering heart home.”
Because perhaps Gomer's most uncomfortable legacy is this:
We kept calling her the scandal until the Gospel showed us that we were the wanderers too—and Christ was the One who came to redeem.
Your worst chapter does not deserve the final word; bring it to the Savior whose scars prove that grace has already written in blood.
